newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan opposition plan more unrest despite deaths.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan opposition plan more unrest despite deaths.

text.p: Opposition-backed groups calling for constitutional reforms in Kenya before this year's general election vowed to stage another protest on Wednesday, after the most violent clashes with police for seven years.

Opposition parties, human rights and church groups in the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) said they would demonstrate at a regional summit in Nairobi -- held to discuss the conflict in Sudan -- to bring Kenya to the attention of visiting leaders.

"Kenya needs conflict management just like Sudan. As a country we don't have the moral authority to tell others how to manage conflict. We will demonstrate, go to where these leaders are meeting, and tell them these things," said NCEC core convenor Kivutha Kibwana.

Kenyan officials ridiculed the NCEC's ability to disrupt President Daniel arap Moi's six-nation summit, which opened at State House on Tuesday and closes on Wednesday morning. They said they expected protest calls to go unheeded.
"What can they achieve? I don't see anyone demonstrating here," said a senior official at heavily-guarded State House.
More than 100 Nairobi University students marched out of their campus late on Tuesday and stoned cars in more than two hours of protest.
They blocked traffic on the main highway through Nairobi until about 70 riot and elite paramilitary General Service Unit police pushed them back, firing baton rounds and teargas.

Later, residents of Nairobi's exclusive Riverside Drive neighbourhood said they heard firing after students again broke out of their residences and police reservists blocked the road into the area. It was unclear what was happening.
Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since unrest in 1991 that helped push Moi to allow multi-party elections.
Security remained tight for the summit. Riot police waited in the rain near the hotels where foreign leaders were staying and patrolled shopping centres around Nairobi wielding pick-axe handles.

"We expect the forthcoming election to be conducted without violence so the Kenyan people can express their democratic verdict. The events over the weekend are yet one further serious blow to that process," British Foreign Office minister Tony Lloyd told parliament on Tuesday.
London-based human rights group Amnesty International deplored Monday's police violence and said those responsible should be brought to justice.

"Excessive violence was clearly used in an attempt to intimidate pro-democracy activists from holding further rallies," Amnesty International said on Tuesday, adding that constitutional reforms after elections would be meaningless.

Reformists want the repeal of six laws that date from colonial times including the Public Order Act used to regulate public gatherings. They are also demanding free access to state-controlled media, particularly radio, and changes in the electoral law.
Police on Tuesday apologised for storming Nairobi's main Anglican All Saints Cathedral where they teargassed and beat up worshippers. They said the incident would be investigated.
The NCEC called for three days of national mourning from Wednesday to Friday for those killed on Monday.

It said it was planning a national strike and holding protests outside provincial administration centres as part of its non-violent campaign to force constitutional changes, which Moi says cannot be introduced before the general election.
No date has been set for the parliamentary and presidential polls in which Moi, 73, is still widely expected to win another five-year term because of squabbling among opposition leaders.
